A representative of the Register yesterday called upon director of the Columbia, Newberry and Laurens Railroad, gentleman who has been from the start most prominently identified with the enterprise, and asked from him a statement of the reasons against consenting to consolidate with the Three C's road understood to be held by the directors of the road first named.

The director approached by the reporter expressed entire willingness to give his view of the situation, which it is understood is that of nearly, if not all, the members of the Board.

First, he said, the proposition made to them by the General Manager of the Three C's was to take their assets and build their road, and he thought they could as well use their own assets as any one else.

In the next place, the director stated that, having organized two years ago last June, they had already graded TWENTY-FIVE miles of road, built piers for bridge across Broad River and graded a mile within the limits of Columbia. This, he thought, was a good proportionate progress as the Three C's itself had made, which had completed only stretch from Camden to York, and another in North Carolina. Their scheme was a grand one, but it has yet to be proved a success by completing the most difficult portion through the mountains, where one mile would cost 500, 80 and other mile sections $50,000 each or thereabouts. If it failed, where would a road consolidated with it be? "Bustled up" was the description of the situation in such an event which he gave.

He did not think the directors would be doing right to expose the road to any such danger, and besides this, without prejudice to the Three C's, there were other roads about as far advanced towards completion as it was, which might be connected with later on, if the Columbia, Newberry and Laurens was left free to choose, and such might prove to be more advantageous than the present proposition. In justice to the interests placed in their care, the directors thought they ought not to act hastily or without due deliberation and consideration of all possibilities.

Continuing, the director said that they had arranged for the timber for the five trestles to be erected in the CITY, that one was already finished, and as soon as all were ready the trestles would at once be built. Then they would go to work saving the Lumber for the superstructure of the bridge, and when that was ready the contract would be awarded indeed, some arrangements had already been made in that direction. The rails to lay the mile of track in the city had also been provided for, and the directors expected to cross Broad River with train by spring.

The timber was sold at fair price, and all the transactions were passed on by the full board of directors.

They had promises of arrangements which would ensure an outlet for the road when completed, and if the Three C's, as stated, were willing to make traffic arrangements for the exchange of freight they would be perfectly willing to do so when the proper time came. the story of the wreck of the English privateer, DE Braak, off Lewes, at the mouth of
Delaware Bay, on June 10, 1858, has been re-
vived by the fitting out of another expedition
to search for the wreck and the millions of
treasure supposed to have gone down with
her. In 1856 Dr. Seth Pancoast of Philadel-
phia, who has become interested in the story
started out to locate the wreck, with the
idea of bringing the sunken treasure to the
surface. He succeeded in finding on the bot-
tom of the ocean, in sixty feet of water, a
mound about 120 feet long by 50 feet wide.
The mound was of sand, while the natural
bottom of the sea is of blue clay. Pancoast
secured the schooner Orr and the tug Startle,
and on July 1, 1881, anchored over the mound.
The two divers were employed and five en-
gines were engaged to furnish air
for the divers and to pump up
brought to the surface. The divers failed to
discover anything of value although pieces
of decayed wood were found in the sand.
The work was continued for about two
months, when the weather became too rough
to continue operation. Pancoast was under
disfied with the divers, believing that they
were not doing honest work. They received
$5 a day for every day they worked, and
two trips a day to the bottom. Pancoast,
who expected to spend $4,000 in the search
had some dispute with the divers about
wages after the work stopped and they sued
him.

The passage by the Legislature of the
bill abolishing the compulsory feature of
the Maryland tobacco inspection and
warehousing system is at last an accom-

plished fact, and removes from this large
and important interest restriction against
which complaint has hitherto been in-
effectual. In the shape the bill goes to the
Governor it secures to the planters the
privilege of storage in the warehouse at
moderate charges, and it leaves them free
to avail themselves of the offices of the

the tobacco interest of the State is a

be too highly commended to the favorable
consideration of the Governor, who ought
to give it his approval, and no doubt will
do so, without moment hesitation.

individual by any arbitrary exercise
of power. The spirit OF the feudal
lords has animated this political
species under all its aliases. In the
DAYS when it was called
the Federal party, it was found at
each step in the framing OF our insti-
tutions, halting between two opinions,
and generally contending for some
semi-monarchical, or semi-despotic
measure. It was always afraid OF the
people, loath to trust the masses to
act directly in their own affairs. These
people would prefer to have halter
round the necks of the populace and
a bit in its mouth by which the
classes of "wealth and intelligence"
might be the better able to guide
affairs into such paths as seemed best
to the few, in spite Of the will OF the
many.


We need not therefore feel
astonished to find the descendants OF
the Federalists in their latest guise and
under their last assumed alias, Repub-
licanism, opposing the proposition to
relegate the election OF our Federal
Senators to direct vote of the peo-
ple. That measure looks to putting a
larger trust in the judgment and hon-
esty of the populace. It looks to
taking the power to manage, direct
and control out of the hands of the
few. It contemplates making it more
difficult for money to assert its sway.
Nor need We be surprised when
the press of this party comes
to discuss this question to find
it going direct to the
writings of the Federalists for their
best reasons for keeping the election
of the Senators where it is. This one
of our Republican contemporaries did
a day or two since. It was quite
right it should. The Federalists are
the grandfathers of the Republicans,
and the family likeness is SO
close that this child knows its
father beyond a question. But
when our Republican neighbor
confuses the proposition of electing
Senators by direct vote with what is
not proposed, the abolition OF the Up-
per House of the National Congress,
he does not disclose any relationship
with the great originators of the
Federal party, Alexander Hamilton
and his confreres. In this bit of reason-
ing he developes features of mental
conformity peculiarly his own, but
features with which we are well
acquainted.
